questions.qtext:
Consider the following statements:
S1 : If all edge costs are equal and positive, then Breadth-First Search (BFS) is optimal.
S2 : Breadth-First Search (BFS) has complete and finite time and space complexity for finite search spaces.
Which of the following is correct?
questions.solution:
(c)
• BFS expands nodes in order of increasing depth. If all edge costs are equal and positive, path cost increases with depth. Hence, BFS returns the solution with the lowest path cost and is optimal. So, S1 is correct.
• BFS is complete in any finite search space because it systematically explores all nodes at each depth level. Its time and space complexity are finite in such spaces, though both can be exponential in the worst case (Ο(bd)). Thus, it guarantees finding a solution if one exists. So, S2
is correct.

Consider the following statements related to Bayesian Networks:
S1 : In a Bayesian network, given its Markov blanket, a node is conditionally independent of all other nodes in the network.
S2 : The Markov blanket of a node consists of all nodes that are reachable within two edges from it.
Which of the following is correct?
questions.solution:
(a)
• Markov blanket of a node includes all the nodes that directly affect it or are affected by it — that means its parents, children, and co-parents (other parents of its children). Once you know these, the node has no influence from the rest of the network. So, S1 is correct.
• “All nodes within two edges” is too broad — some of those nodes may have no role in influencing the node. The Markov blanket depends on relationships, not just distance. So, S2 is incorrect.

Consider the following statements:
S1 : Beam Search is not guaranteed to find a solution even if one exists, due to its limited beam width.
S2 : Beam Search is a greedy algorithm when the beam width is set to 1.
Which of the following is correct?
questions.solution:
(c)
• Beam Search limits the number of nodes explored at each level. If the optimal path is outside the top-k nodes, it may be pruned, and no solution will be found-even if one exists. So, S1 is correct. • When the beam width is set to 1, beam search behaves like Greedy Best-First Search. It always
expands the single best-looking node based on the heuristic, ignoring all others. So, S2 is correct.

Consider the following statements:
S1 : Belief Propagation performs exact inference only on a single tree-structured graph.
S2 : Gibbs Sampling guarantees exact results in finite time.
Which of the following is/are correct?
questions.solution:
(a)
• Belief Propagation gives exact results only on tree-structured graphs, it requires the graph to be a single connected acyclic structure (a tree), If the graph has loops, it becomes approximate (Loopy BP). So, S1 is correct.
• Gibbs Sampling is a stochastic sampling-based method (MCMC), it does not provide exact results in finite time, Exactness is only achieved asymptotically with infinite samples under certain conditions. So, S2 is correct.

questions.qtext: Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: In Greedy Best-First Search, the node to be expanded next is selected based on the lowest heuristic estimate of the distance to the goal node.
In Greedy Best-First Search, the node to be expanded next is selected based on the highest heuristic estimate of the distance to the goal node.
Uniform Cost Search expands the node with the lowest heuristic value to the goal.

questions.solution:
(a)
• Greedy Best-First Search selects the node with the lowest heuristic value h(n), which estimates
the cost to reach the goal. It ignores the path cost from the start node (g(n)). So, option (a) is
correct and option (b) is incorrect.
• Uniform Cost Search selects the node with the lowest path cost from the start node (g(n)), not
based on the heuristic estimate to the goal. Hence, it does not use h(n). So, option (c) is
incorrect.

Consider the following statements:
S1 : Beam Search algorithm takes the same amount of space as Breadth-First Search (BFS).
S2 : Best-First Search algorithm takes less space compared to Beam Search.
Which of the following is correct?
questions.solution:
(d)
• Breadth-First Search (BFS) stores all nodes at the current level, which can result in exponential space complexity in the worst case.
Beam Search stores only the top k best nodes per level (where k is the beam width), thereby reducing space usage significantly. So, S1 is incorrect.
• Best-First Search: Uses a priority queue and can store many generated nodes — space usage can be large.
Beam Search: Stores only a fixed number (beam width) of best candidates, making it more memory-efficient. So, S2 is incorrect.

questions.qtext: Consider a search tree where all actions have unit step cost and multiple goal nodes may exist at different depths. If Breadth-First Search (BFS) is used to find a goal node, which of the following is guaranteed to be true?

options.text: BFS will always find the leftmost goal node.
BFS may miss the shallowest goal node if it's not on the left.
BFS will always find the goal node that is shallowest (least depth).
BFS does not guarantee goal finding if the search tree is infinite.

questions.solution:
(c)
• BFS selects nodes based on depth, not left/right position. If a deeper goal is on the left, BFS may still choose a shallower goal elsewhere. So, option (a) is incorrect.
• BFS explores all nodes at the current depth before going deeper, so it cannot miss the shallowest goal. So, option (b) is incorrect.
• BFS expands nodes level by level, it is guaranteed to find the first goal at the lowest depth. So, option (c) is correct.
• If the goal is at finite depth, BFS will reach it even in an infinite tree. Only DFS can get stuck in infinite branches, not BFS. So, option (d) is incorrect.

questions.qtext: Which of the following statements is/are correct?

options.text: Exact inference in Bayesian networks is always tractable when the network is a polytree.
The presence of undirected cycles in a Bayesian network can lead to exponential inference complexity.
Polytrees support exact marginal computation using message passing in constant time.

questions.solution:
(b)
• Although polytrees (singly connected DAGs) allow for tractable inference using belief propagation, tractability is not unconditional.
Algorithmic complexity still scales linearly with network size; thus, the term “always tractable” is an over generalization. So, option (a) is incorrect.
• In multiply connected Bayesian networks (with undirected cycles), inference requires computational resources that grow exponentially in the worst case.
This problem is proven to be NP-hard, due to the combinatorial explosion of joint dependencies.
So, option (b) is correct.
• While belief propagation enables exact inference in polytrees, the run time is linear in the
number of nodes and edges.
Claiming it works in constant time is incorrect, as complexity still depends on the network’s topological structure. So, option (c) is incorrect.

questions.qtext: Which of the following statements is/are correct?

options.text: Iterative Deepening DFS performs search limited to a predefined depth.
Breadth First Search explores all nodes at a level before going to the next, it is use a predefined depth limit.
Depth-Limited Search may fail to find the solution if the depth limit is set too

questions.solution:
(a, c)
• Iterative Deepening DFS (IDDFS) combines the benefits of DFS and BFS. It performs depthlimited searches repeatedly, increasing the limit one level at a time. At each iteration, it uses a fixed predefined depth. So, option (a) is correct.
• BFS explores all nodes at a particular depth level before moving to the next. It continues until the goal is found and does not stop at any predefined depth, unlike Depth-Limited Search.
So, option (b) is incorrect.
• DLS restricts the search to a fixed depth. If the goal node lies beyond this limit, it will not be
explored — causing the search to fail even if the goal is reachable. So, option (c) is correct.

questions.qtext:
Consider the following statements:
S1 : Stochastic simulation relies on generating random samples to approximate outcomes in probabilistic systems where analytical solutions are hard.
S2 : Monte Carlo sampling estimates numerical results, such as expectations or integrals, through repeated random trials.
S3 : In high-dimensional problems, advanced methods like importance sampling or MCMC enhance efficiency by focusing on high-probability regions.
Which of the following above statements is correct?
questions.solution:
(d)
• Stochastic simulation indeed uses random sampling to model or approximate systems where exact analytic computation is difficult or intractable. So, S1 is correct.
• Monte Carlo methods are classic stochastic techniques for estimating numerical values (like expected values or integrals) using repeated random sampling. So, S2 is correct.
• In high-dimensional spaces, naive random sampling becomes inefficient. Methods like Importance Sampling and Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) are used to concentrate sampling in more relevant, high-probability regions-thereby increasing efficiency and accuracy.
So, S3 is correct.

questions.qtext: Which of the following statements about Beam Search is/are correct?

options.text: Beam Search is a heuristic search algorithm that maintains only a fixed number of best nodes at each level.
Beam Search is complete and optimal only when the beam width is large enough to include all possible nodes at each level.
Beam Search expands all nodes at each level and then selects the k best without regard to memory constraints.
Beam Search may discard the optimal path if it is not among the top-k nodes at any level.

questions.solution:
(a, b, d)
• Beam Search is a heuristic search that selects only the top-k scoring nodes at each level. This reduces memory usage while guiding the search using a heuristic function. So, option (a) is correct.
• Beam Search becomes complete and optimal only if the beam width is large enough to cover all nodes. In that case, it behaves like Breadth-First Search and does not miss any paths. So, option (b) is correct.
• Beam Search does not expand all nodes at each level. It evaluates all, but then keeps only the
best k nodes, limiting memory. So, option (c) is incorrect.
• Beam Search may discard the optimal path if it is not in the top-k at any level. Once a path is
pruned, it is never reconsidered — even if it could lead to the goal So, option (d) is correct.

questions.qtext: Which of the following statements is/are correct?

options.text: Variable ordering has no effect on the complexity of inference algorithms.
The optimal variable ordering minimizes the size of intermediate factors.
Junction tree construction is independent of variable ordering.
Identifying relevant variables before inference can reduce computation.

questions.solution:
(b, d)
• Variable ordering has a major impact on inference complexity in algorithms like variable
elimination and junction tree.
A poor ordering can result in large intermediate factors, increasing time and space requirements.
So, option (a) is incorrect.
• The size of intermediate factors created during variable elimination depends on the variable
elimination order.
An optimal ordering minimizes these sizes, improving computational efficiency.
This is key to keeping inference tractable in large graphs. So, option (b) is correct.
• Junction Tree construction involves moralization and triangulation, which are affected by the
elimination order.
Different orderings can result in different tree widths, impacting the efficiency of message
passing.
So, variable ordering does influence junction tree construction. So, option (c) is incorrect.
• If a variable is irrelevant (i.e., conditionally independent of the query given evidence), it
doesn’t affect the result.
Removing such variables reduces the number of nodes in the graph.
This simplifies the model and saves computational effort during inference. So, option (d) is
correct.
